title: Food for the bereaved
hook: make food for the family of Ja'far, for what has come to them (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday, three days, and Umm Habibah's perfume on the third. Your line: three days of mourning. Did you send someone a message that asked nothing back? Today closes the week with a pot on the stove. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

A casserole dish with masking tape on the bottom and a name written in marker. A tray of rice left on a doorstep. A neighbor who doesn't knock, just texts: it's outside. Some grieving households end up with a kitchen full of other people's cooking. In Islam, that habit has a sentence behind it, and a name. The name is Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin. When the news of his death reached Madinah, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, didn't give a speech. He gave an instruction about dinner.
screen: `A DISH WITH A NAME ON THE BOTTOM.` → `NEWS OF JA'FAR.` → `AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT DINNER.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, told by Ja'far's son 'Abdullah. When the news of Ja'far's death came, the Prophet said, in paraphrase: make food for the family of Ja'far, for something has come to them that keeps them busy. Look at the reason he gives. Not that they're sad, though they were. That they're occupied. A death takes over a household. There's the washing, the shroud, the prayer and the burial you've walked through this week, the visitors, the phone calls, the children who need explaining to. Nobody in that house is thinking about lunch, and somebody has to. So the instruction lands on the neighbors, not the family. The ones who grieve are fed. Jurists later drew a quiet lesson from the same hadith: the burden runs one way. The neighbors cook for the bereaved household, and the household isn't put to the work and expense of feeding a crowd. Now step back and see the whole week. At the deathbed, gentle words said softly. The body washed with care. Everyone in the same white shroud. The community standing in prayer. The grave, facing the qiblah. Three days with a door out. And now, a pot of food carried across the street. Look how much of it is done with hands and feet rather than speeches: washing, wrapping, standing, digging, cooking. In these texts, much of the way through a death is a list of tasks, done for someone who can't do them right now. A pot of rice, left on a step.
screen: `MAKE FOOD FOR JA'FAR'S FAMILY.` · `THEY ARE OCCUPIED.` · `THE NEIGHBORS COOK.` · `A WEEK OF THINGS DONE BY HAND.`

segments.voice: The practice: take food to a grieving family, starting here, in your head. Settle and breathe. Is there a household you know that is carrying a loss, this month or this year? If one comes to mind, think what they might actually eat. Something simple. Something that keeps. Picture the dish, and the doorstep, and leaving it without needing to be thanked. If no one comes to mind, think back over the week's line: soft words, careful hands, white cloth, standing, earth, three days, food. Let one of them stay with you. The bell holds the time.
Food for the bereaved. The Prophet's instruction to cook for a grieving family, because what has come to them keeps them busy. Today's word.

Your line: feed the grieving. If you know someone in loss, send food or plan when you'll take it. If not, make one extra portion of dinner and give it away. Tomorrow, tears are mercy. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslim neighbors and relatives bring meals to a bereaved household in the first days after a death, following the hadith in Abu Dawud about the family of Ja'far, so the family doesn't have to cook or host.

original.note: Arabic: food, a meal, as given and shared.

trapdoor: what you thought: bringing food after a death is just a nice custom.
what it means: the Prophet told people to cook for Ja'far's family because their loss kept them occupied.
what a scholar hears: Abu Dawud's hadith from 'Abdullah ibn Ja'far, and jurists reading it as: the neighbors feed the household, not the other way round.

notes: Editor: removed the unsourced claim that cooking was the Prophet's first response ('he started with dinner', 'first instruction'); the week look-back no longer says every practice is done by hand (deathbed words and the standing prayer are not); ended on a concrete image instead of uplift.
Abu Dawud 3132 paraphrased; confirm number, narrator ('Abdullah ibn Ja'far), and the news reaching Madinah.
The jurists' point (the family should not bear the cost of feeding guests) is stated generally; some cite a report of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah in Ibn Majah. Confirm phrasing.
The tomorrow title 'Tears are mercy' is in the close; week look-back covers days 1338–1344.
